"One JACK client for a chain: what it saves and what it does not"

Running N plugins in series inside one JACK client, instead of N clients linked in series, is bit-identical and cuts the cycle's end time by 30 to 56 % at the median and the host's CPU by a third or more, with no xrun and no worse tail; the saving is the wake-ups, not the plugins.
A 4-CPU Fedora 44 container on a shared machine, PipeWire 1.6.9 on its dummy driver, 48 and 96 kHz at 64 and 128 frames, October 2026; omx-plugins 0.12.0 and stock LV2 and CLAP plugins.
A chain of LV2 plugins needs a union world

The question

omx-clap-host gives every plugin its own JACK client, and every client is a node of the graph with its own wake-up per cycle. The question was whether N plugins in series in one client are bit-identical with the same N plugins in N clients linked in series, and whether the bench's numbers get better, with nothing getting worse. This is the measurement behind the chain of the host library (see the chains note for how plugin-hostd uses it).

How the chain runs

  • The head is an instance with its own client, ports and process callback. The members open no client and register no port: their cycles run inside the head's.
  • A member is accepted only when its main inputs are as wide as the previous member's outputs and its main outputs as wide as the head's. A plugin with a note input or output is not accepted as a member. A member's auxiliary inputs read silence.
  • The head's process callback runs the head, then each member in order, each inside its own cycle gate, handing each output buffer to the next; the last member writes the head's output ports. Between them the outputs are 64-byte aligned blocks the host holds.
  • Every member's audio thread is the head's; its block size and transport follow the head's.
  • The head's ports report the sum of every member's latency on top of its own, recomputed when any member's latency changes.
  • Bypass, parameters, meters, pins, presets and state stay per instance, by the member's own number.
  • Removing a member unlinks it inside a gate of the chain's own, between cycles; removing the head frees every member with it.

Bit identity

One host with the plugins in N clients in series, one with them in a chain, both fed the same deterministic noise and recorded from the same cycles, left and right: every pair compared sample by sample, and the latency each arm's last output reports compared. A control pass first runs two N-client arms against each other, so a plugin that is not deterministic between two instances of itself shows there, not as the chain's difference. 48 kHz, quantum 1024, 96 000 samples per side:

  • The two reverbs, Dragonfly Room and caps PlateX2, are not deterministic between two instances of themselves (two one-client-per-plugin arms differ at about -30 dB), so with either in the set no arm can be judged sample by sample: the chain's difference is the control's size. Every other plugin of the table is bit-identical through the chain.
  • The compressor rounded one ulp apart (-142 dB) between two instances now and then, chain or not; with the blocks 64-byte aligned the chain was identical.
  • The latency the chain reports is the members' sum: three passthroughs of 64 frames report 192.
  • Sabotaged, the test goes red: with the members skipped the output differs at sample 0, and with the latency sum dropped the chain reports 64 against 192.

A chain of LV2 plugins needs a union world

plugin-hostd narrows a worker's LV2_PATH to the plugin's own bundle, and an LV2 plugin is found on that path when it is added. A chain's members are added in the head's process, with the head's LV2_PATH: in a world of the first plugin's bundle alone, the second member answers resp -101 (not found). A chain of LV2 plugins therefore needs its worker's LV2_PATH to be the union of its members' bundles, and nothing wider. The pins need nothing new: each member's add checks its own layout, and with pins on, every member of the 7- and 8-plugin LV2 chains refused a wrong pin and took its right one; the pinned chain was bit-identical with the pinned series.

  • The cycle's end falls 30 to 56 % at the median and 21 to 49 % at the 99th percentile; repetition by repetition, the chain's worst is below the series' best in every row.
  • No xrun in any run of either arm. Overruns fall in ten rows of twelve; in two four-plugin rows the chain's median is one overrun higher (12 against 11, 5 against 4, out of about 22 500 and 11 250 cycles), within the spread of the repetitions.
  • The chain's one node waits for its wake-up as long as the series' first node, or longer, and then runs the whole series without another wake-up: that is where the saving is.
  • The host's CPU falls by a third or more, and its memory by 4 to 9 MiB: N-1 JACK clients fewer, their threads and buffers.

What was not measured

The container had no /dev/cpu_dma_latency, so no CPU idle-state hold was in effect (see CPU idle states and plugin hosting), and its real-time limit was 0, so PipeWire's threads ran SCHED_OTHER: the figures are larger and noisier than a real-time graph's, the same for both arms. Whether part of the saving is the idle-state exit stays open until the same bench runs on a machine with the device, at each hold.
